danishChanges.before: fortrinet for menneskelig velstand. De lande, hvori bogstaver og kunst har blomstret, er blevet for meget beundret, fordi det skjulte mål for deres dyrkning ikke er blevet forstået, og deres skæbnesvangre virkninger ikke taget i betragtning. »Idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset.« [»Tåber kaldte det 'menneskelighed', hvad var en del af trældom,« Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Skal vi aldrig se i de maksimer, bøger nedlægger, den vulgære interesse, der driver deres forfattere? Nej: hvad de end siger, så er det ikke sandt, at alt står vel til, når et land trods sit ry er affolket, og det er ikke nok, at en digter har en indkomst på 100.000 franc, til at gøre hans tidsalder til den bedste af alle. Mindre opmærksomhed bør lægges på herskernes tilsyneladende hvile og ro end på deres nationers velvære som helheder, og frem for alt på de mest folkerige stater. En haglstorm hærger flere kantoner, men medfører sjældent en hungersnød. Udbrud og borgerkrige giver herskere hårde stød, men de er ikke folkenes virkelige onder, der endda kan få et pusterum, mens der strides om, hvem der skal tyrannisere dem. Deres sande velstand og ulykker kommer af deres permanente tilstand: det er, når helheden forbliver knust under åget, at forfaldet sætter ind, og herskerne efter behag ødelægger folket, og »ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant« [»Hvor de skaber en ørken, kalder de det fred,« Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Da de stores stridigheder forstyrrede Frankrigs kongerige, og koadjutoren i Paris bar en daggert i lommen til parlamentet, hindrede disse ting ikke det franske folk i at blomstre og formere sig i værdighed, lethed og frihed. For længe siden blomstrede Grækenland midt under de mest vilde krige; blod flød i strømme, og dog var hele landet fuldt af indbyggere. Det syntes, siger Machiavelli, at vor republik midt under mord, proskription og borgerkrig kun trivedes: borgernes dyd, moral og uafhængighed gjorde mere for at styrke den, end alle deres uoverensstemmelser gjorde for at svække den. En lille uro giver sjælen elasticitet; det, der gør slægten virkelig velstående, er ikke så meget fred som frihed.

danishChanges.before: Sådan er den naturlige og uundgåelige tendens selv hos de bedst forfattede regeringer. Hvis Sparta og Roma gik til grunde, hvilken stat kan da håbe at vare evigt? danishChanges.before: Den politiske krop, som den menneskelige krop, begynder at dø, så snart den er født, og bærer i sig selv årsagerne til sin ødelæggelse. Men hver kan have en forfatning mere eller mindre robust, mere eller mindre egnet til at bevare den i kortere eller længere tid. Menneskets forfatning er naturens værk; statens er kunstens værk. Det står ikke i menneskenes magt at forlænge deres egne liv; men det står i deres magt at forlænge statens liv så meget som muligt ved at give den den bedst mulige forfatning. Den bedst forfattede stat vil have en ende; men den vil ende senere end nogen anden, medmindre en uforudset tilfældighed bringer dens utidige ødelæggelse.
danishChanges.after: Statslegemet, som den menneskelige krop, begynder at dø, så snart den er født, og bærer i sig selv årsagerne til sin ødelæggelse. danishChanges.before: Den politiske krops livsprincip ligger i den suveræne myndighed. Den lovgivende magt er statens hjerte; den udøvende magt er dens hjerne, der sætter alle delene i bevægelse. Hjernen kan være lammet, og enkeltpersonen leve videre. En mand kan forblive en idiot og leve; men så snart hjertet ophører med at udføre sine funktioner, er dyret dødt.

danishChanges.before: Hvorfor vises der da så megen respekt for gamle love? Af netop denne grund. Vi må tro, at intet andet end de gamle viljeshandlingers fortrinlighed kan have bevaret dem så længe: hvis suverænen ikke havde anerkendt dem som sunde hele vejen igennem, ville den have tilbagekaldt dem tusinde gange. Det er derfor lovene, langt fra at blive svage, uafladeligt vinder ny styrke i enhver velforfattet stat; antikkens forrang gør dem dagligt mere ærværdige. Hvor lovene tværtimod bliver svage, efterhånden som de bliver gamle, beviser dette, at der ikke længere er nogen lovgivende magt, og at staten er død.
danishChanges.after: Hvorfor vises der da så megen respekt for gamle love? Af netop denne grund. danishChanges.before: Suverænen, der ikke har anden magt end den lovgivende, handler kun ved hjælp af lovene; og da lovene intet andet er end almenviljens autentiske handlinger, kan suverænen ikke handle, undtagen når folket er forsamlet. Folket i forsamling, vil man sige til mig, er en ren chimære. Det er den i dag, men for to tusind år siden var den det ikke. Har menneskets natur ændret sig?

Men hvordan kan små stater gives styrke til at modstå store, sådan som de græske byer engang modstod Storkongen, og som Holland og Schweiz for nylig har modstået huset Østrig?

Når borgerne er griske, fejge og forsagte og elsker mageligheden mere end friheden, holder de ikke længe stand mod regeringens fordoblede anstrengelser; og således, efterhånden som den modstående kraft uafladeligt vokser, ender den suveræne myndighed med at forsvinde, og de fleste byer falder og går til grunde før deres tid.

I et land, der er virkeligt frit, gør borgerne alt med deres egne arme og intet ved penge; langt fra at betale for at blive fritaget for deres pligter ville de endda betale for privilegiet at opfylde dem selv. danishChanges.before: Suveræniteten kan af samme grund, der gør den uafhændelig, ikke repræsenteres; den ligger væsentligt i almenviljen, og en vilje tillader ikke repræsentation: den er enten den samme eller en anden; der er ingen mellemmulighed. Folkets deputerede er da ikke og kan ikke være dets repræsentanter; de er blot dets forvaltere og kan ikke gennemføre nogen endelige handlinger. Enhver lov, folket ikke har stadfæstet personligt, er ugyldig — er faktisk ingen lov. Englands folk anser sig selv for frit, men det tager grueligt fejl: det er kun frit under valget af parlamentsmedlemmer. Så snart de er valgt, indhenter trældommen det, og det er intet. Den brug, det gør af de korte øjeblikke af frihed, det nyder, viser, at det fortjener at miste dem.

Enhver lov, folket ikke har stadfæstet personligt, er ugyldig — er faktisk ingen lov. Den brug, det gør af de korte øjeblikke af frihed, det nyder, viser, at det fortjener at miste dem.
reasons: French-source fidelity, idiomatic modern Danish and restoration of author notes

danishChanges.before: Idéen om repræsentation er moderne; den kommer til os fra feudal regering — fra det uretfærdige og absurde system, der nedværdiger menneskeheden og vanærer menneskenavnet. I oldtidens republikker, og selv i monarkier, havde folket aldrig repræsentanter; selve ordet var ukendt. Det er højst påfaldende, at i Roma, hvor tribunerne var så ukrænkelige, blev det aldrig så meget som tænkt, at de kunne tilrane sig folkets funktioner, og at de midt i en så stor mængde aldrig forsøgte at vedtage et eneste plebiscitum på egen myndighed. Vi kan dog få et indtryk af de vanskeligheder, der til tider opstod ved, at folket var så talrigt, ud fra hvad der skete på Gracchernes tid, da nogle af borgerne måtte afgive deres stemmer fra bygningernes tagrygge.

danishChanges.before: Men for at forklare, hvordan tribunerne undertiden virkelig repræsenterede folket, er det nok at fatte, hvordan regeringen repræsenterer suverænen. Da loven er rent og skært erklæringen af almenviljen, er det klart, at folket ikke kan repræsenteres ved udøvelsen af lovgivende magt; men ved udøvelsen af udøvende magt, der kun er den styrke, der anvendes til at give loven virkning, kan og bør det både repræsenteres. Vi ser således, at hvis vi nøje undersøgte sagen, ville vi finde, at meget få nationer overhovedet har love. Hvordan det end forholder sig, er det sikkert, at tribunerne, der ingen udøvende magt havde, aldrig ved ret af de magter, der var dem betroet, kunne repræsentere det romerske folk, men kun ved at tilrane sig senatets.
danishChanges.after: Men for at forklare, hvordan tribunerne undertiden virkelig repræsenterede folket, er det nok at fatte, hvordan regeringen repræsenterer suverænen. danishChanges.before: I Grækenland gjorde folket alt, hvad det havde at gøre, selv; det var uafladeligt forsamlet på det offentlige torv. Grækerne levede i et mildt klima; de havde ingen naturlig grådighed; slaver gjorde deres arbejde for dem; deres store anliggende var friheden. Når I mangler de samme fordele, hvordan kan I bevare de samme rettigheder? Jeres barskere klimaer øger jeres behov;[1] i halvdelen af året er jeres offentlige torve ubeboelige; jeres sprogs fladhed gør dem uegnede til at høres i det fri; I ofrer mere for profit end for frihed og frygter trældom mindre end fattigdom.
danishChanges.after: I Grækenland gjorde folket alt, hvad det havde at gøre, selv; det var uafladeligt forsamlet på det offentlige torv. Jeres barskere klimaer øger jeres behov;[1] i halvdelen af året er jeres offentlige torve umulige at opholde sig på; jeres sprogs fladhed gør dem uegnede til at høres i det fri; I ofrer mere for profit end for frihed og frygter trældom mindre end fattigdom.

danishChanges.before: Hvad da? Opretholdes friheden kun ved hjælp af slaveri? Måske. Yderpunkter mødes. Alt, hvad der ikke er i naturens gang, har sine ulemper, det borgerlige samfund mest af alt. Der er nogle uheldige omstændigheder, hvorunder vi kun kan bevare vor frihed på andres bekostning, og hvor borgeren kun kan være fuldkomment fri, når slaven er mest slave. Sådan var det i Sparta. Hvad jer angår, moderne folk, har I ingen slaver, men I er selv slaver; I betaler deres frihed med jeres egen. Forgæves praler I med dette fortrin; jeg finder mere fejhed end menneskelighed i det.
danishChanges.after: Hvad da? Opretholdes friheden kun ved hjælp af slaveri? Måske. Yderpunkter mødes. Alt, hvad der ikke er i naturens gang, har sine ulemper, det borgerlige samfund mest af alt. danishChanges.before: Jeg mener ikke med alt dette, at det er nødvendigt at have slaver, eller at slaveri-retten er legitim; jeg giver blot grundene til, at moderne folk, der tror sig frie, har repræsentanter, mens oldtidens folk ikke havde nogen. I alle tilfælde, det øjeblik et folk lader sig repræsentere, er det ikke længere frit: det eksisterer ikke længere.
danishChanges.after: Jeg mener ikke med alt dette, at det er nødvendigt at have slaver, eller at retten til slaveri er legitim, for jeg har bevist det modsatte; jeg giver blot grundene til, at moderne folk, der tror sig frie, har repræsentanter, mens oldtidens folk ikke havde nogen. danishChanges.before: Alt taget i betragtning ser jeg ikke, hvordan det fra nu af er muligt for suverænen at bevare blandt os udøvelsen af sine rettigheder, medmindre byen er meget lille. Men hvis den er meget lille, vil den så ikke blive erobret? Nej. Jeg vil senere vise, hvordan et stort folks ydre styrke[2] kan kombineres med en lille stats bekvemme statsforfatning og gode orden.
danishChanges.after: Alt taget i betragtning ser jeg ikke, hvordan det fra nu af er muligt for suverænen at bevare blandt os udøvelsen af sine rettigheder, medmindre bystaten er meget lille. danishChanges.before: Når den lovgivende magt er fast etableret, er det næste at etablere den udøvende magt på samme måde; for den udøvende magt, der kun virker ved særhandlinger, er ikke af den lovgivendes væsen og er naturligt adskilt fra den. Hvis det var muligt for suverænen som sådan at besidde den udøvende magt, ville ret og kendsgerning være så forvirret, at ingen kunne sige, hvad der var lov, og hvad der ikke var; og den politiske krop, således vansiret, ville snart blive bytte for selve den vold, den blev indstiftet til at forhindre.
danishChanges.after: Når den lovgivende magt er fast etableret, er det næste at etablere den udøvende magt på samme måde; for den udøvende magt, der kun virker ved enkelthandlinger, er ikke af den lovgivendes væsen og er naturligt adskilt fra den. Hvis det var muligt for suverænen som sådan at besidde den udøvende magt, ville ret og kendsgerning være så sammenblandet, at ingen kunne sige, hvad der var lov, og hvad der ikke var; og statslegemet, hvis natur således var forvansket, ville snart blive bytte for selve den vold, den blev indstiftet til at forhindre.

danishChanges.after: Da borgerne ved samfundskontrakten alle er lige, kan alle foreskrive, hvad alle bør gøre, men ingen har ret til at kræve, at en anden gør, hvad han selv ikke gør. danishChanges.before: Det er blevet hævdet, at denne handling af oprettelse var en kontrakt mellem folket og de herskere, det sætter over sig — en kontrakt, der fastlægger vilkår, der binder den ene side til at befale og den anden til at adlyde. Dette er, jeg er sikker på, det vil blive indrømmet, en mærkelig slags kontrakt at indgå. Men lad os se, om denne opfattelse kan opretholdes.
danishChanges.after: Det er blevet hævdet, at denne oprettelseshandling var en kontrakt mellem folket og de herskere, det sætter over sig — en kontrakt, der fastlægger vilkår, der binder den ene side til at befale og den anden til at adlyde. Da den mand, der har magten til sin rådighed, altid er i stand til at kontrollere udførelsen, ville det komme ud på det samme, hvis vi kaldte en handling, hvor en mand siger til en anden: »Jeg giver dig alle mine goder på den betingelse, at du giver mig så meget af dem tilbage, som du ønsker,« for en »kontrakt«.
danishChanges.after: Det er også indlysende, at de kontraherende parter, indbyrdes, kun ville være under naturloven uden nogen garantier for deres gensidige forpligtelser — en stilling, der fuldstændig er i strid med samfundstilstanden. danishChanges.before: Dette ændrede forhold er ingen spekulativ subtilitet uden praktiske eksempler: det sker hver dag i det engelske parlament, hvor underhuset ved visse lejligheder konstituerer sig som Grand Committee, til den bedre drøftelse af forretningerne, og således, efter at have været en suveræn ret i ét øjeblik, i det næste bliver en blot kommission. Det rapporterer derefter tilbage til sig selv, som underhus, resultatet af sine forhandlinger i Grand Committee og debatterer på ny under ét navn, hvad det allerede har afgjort under et andet.

Det er umuligt at oprette regering på nogen anden måde legitimt og i overensstemmelse med de hidtil opstillede principper.

danishChanges.before: Hvad vi netop har sagt, bekræfter kapitel XVI og gør det klart, at regeringens indstiftelse ikke er en kontrakt, men en lov; at de betroede af den udøvende magt ikke er folkets herrer, men dets embedsmænd; at det kan oprette dem og fjerne dem, som det vil; at der for dem ikke er tale om kontrakt, men om lydighed; og at de, ved at påtage sig de funktioner, staten pålægger dem, intet andet gør end at opfylde deres pligt som borgere uden nogen ret til at strides om betingelserne.

danishChanges.before: Det er også sandt, at man i sådanne tilfælde ikke kan være for omhyggelig med at iagttage alle de formaliteter, der kræves for at skelne en regelmæssig og legitim handling fra en opviglerisk tumult, og et helt folks vilje fra en fraktions klamren. Her frem for alt bør der ikke gives nogen yderligere indrømmelse til den ubekvemme mulighed, end hvad strengt logisk ikke kan nægtes. Af denne forpligtelse drager fyrsten en stor fordel ved at holde sin magt mod folket, uden at nogen kan sige, at han har tilrøvet sig den. Idet han synes kun at gøre brug af sine rettigheder, finder han det meget let at udvide dem og — under påskud af at bevare freden — at hindre forsamlinger, hvis formål er at genoprette ordenen. Således udnytter han en tavshed, han ikke tillader at blive brudt, eller uregelmæssigheder, han selv forårsager, til at antage, at han har støtte fra dem, frygten holder fra at tale, og til at straffe dem, der vover at tale. Sådan var det, at decemvirerne, der først blev valgt for ét år og derefter beholdt for et andet, forsøgte at gøre deres magt evigtvarende ved at forbyde comitierne at forsamles. Ved denne lette metode tilrøver enhver regering i verden, når først den er klædt i offentlig magt, før eller siden den suveræne myndighed.

danishChanges.before: Jeg antager her, hvad jeg tror at have vist — at der i staten ikke findes nogen grundlov, der ikke kan ophæves, ikke engang selve samfundskontrakten; for hvis alle borgerne forsamledes med ét sind for at bryde kontrakten, er det umuligt at tvivle på, at den meget legitimt ville blive brudt. Grotius mener endda, at hver mand kan give afkald på sit medlemskab af sin egen stat og generobre sin naturlige frihed og sine goder ved at forlade landet.[1] Det ville faktisk være absurd, hvis alle borgerne i forsamling ikke kunne gøre, hvad hver kan gøre på egen hånd.

Grotius mener endda, at enhver kan give afkald på sit medlemskab af sin egen stat og generobre sin naturlige frihed og sine goder ved at forlade landet.[1] Det ville faktisk være absurd, hvis alle borgerne i forsamling ikke kunne gøre, hvad hver kan gøre på egen hånd.

danishChanges.before: Følger det heraf, at almenviljen er udslettet eller fordærvet? Slet ikke: den er altid bestandig, uforanderlig og ren; men den er underordnet andre viljer, der trænger ind på dens område. Hver mand, der løsriver sin interesse fra den fælles interesse, ser klart, at han ikke helt kan adskille dem; men hans andel i de offentlige ulykker synes ham ubetydelig sammenlignet med det udelukkende gode, han sigter mod at gøre til sit eget. Bortset fra dette særlige gode vil han det almene gode i sin egen interesse lige så stærkt som nogen anden. Selv ved at sælge sin stemme for penge slukker han ikke almenviljen i sig — han undgår den blot. Den fejl, han begår, er at ændre spørgsmålet og at svare noget andet, end hvad han bliver spurgt om. I stedet for ved sin stemme at sige: »Det er til statens fordel,« siger han: »Det er til denne eller hin mands eller partis fordel, at denne eller hin opfattelse skal sejre.« Så loven om offentlig orden i forsamlinger er ikke så meget at opretholde almenviljen i dem som at sikre, at spørgsmålet altid stilles til den, og svaret altid gives af den.

danishChanges.before: Da alle Romas mest berømmelige borgere boede på markerne og dyrkede jorden, vænnede mænd sig til at se dér alene efter republikkens grundpiller. Denne levevis, der var de bedste patricieres, blev æret af alle; landsbymandens enkle, arbejdsomme liv blev foretrukket frem for Romas _bourgeoisie_'s dovne og uvirksomme liv; og en mand, der i byen kun ville have været en elendig proletar, blev som markarbejder en agtet borger. Ikke uden grund, siger Varro, oprettede vore storsindede forfædre i landsbyen planteskolen for de robuste og tapre mænd, der forsvarede dem i krigens tid og skaffede dem deres underhold i fredstid. Plinius slår positivt fast, at landstammerne blev æret på grund af de mænd, der udgjorde dem; mens kujoner, som mænd ønskede at vanære, som offentlig vanære blev overført til bystammerne. Sabineren Appius Claudius, da han kom for at bosætte sig i Roma, blev overøst med æresbevisninger og indskrevet i en landstamme, der senere antog hans familienavn. Endelig kom frigivne altid ind i bystammerne, aldrig i landstammerne; ej heller findes der gennem hele republikken et eneste eksempel på, at en frigiven, selv om han var blevet borger, nåede noget magistratembede.

Han gav derfor folket gennem denne forsamling al antallets myndighed for at opveje magtens og rigdommenes, som han overlod til patricierne. danishChanges.before: Opdelingen efter centurier var så gunstig for aristokratiet, at det ved første øjekast er svært at se, hvordan senatet nogensinde undlod at vinde dagen i de comitier, der bar deres navn, og hvori konsulerne, censorerne og de andre kuruliske magistrater blev valgt. Faktisk indeholdt den første klasse af de hundrede og treoghalvfems centurier, hvori hele det romerske folks seks klasser var opdelt, otteoghalvfems; og da der udelukkende blev stemt efter centurier, havde denne klasse alene flertal over alle de øvrige. Når alle disse centurier var enige, blev resten af stemmerne ikke engang taget; det mindste antals afgørelse gik for at være mængdens, og det kan siges, at i _Comitia Centuriata_ blev afgørelser bestemt langt mere af pungens dybde end af antallet af stemmer.

danishChanges.before: _Comitia Tributa_ var i egentlig forstand det romerske folks råd. De blev sammenkaldt af tribunerne alene; i dem blev tribunerne valgt og vedtog deres plebiscita. Senatet havde ikke alene ingen status i dem, men ingen ret end ikke til at være til stede; og senatorerne, der var tvunget til at adlyde love, de ikke kunne stemme om, var i denne henseende mindre frie end de ringeste borgere. Denne uretfærdighed var fuldstændig forfejlet og var alene nok til at ugyldiggøre dekreter fra et organ, hvortil ikke alle dets medlemmer var indladt. Hvis alle patricierne havde været til stede ved comitierne i kraft af den ret, de havde som borgere, ville de som blotte privatpersoner ikke have haft nogen betydelig indflydelse på en stemmegivning, der blev talt efter hoveder, hvor den ringeste proletar var lige så god som _princeps senatus_.

Denne skik var god, så længe ærlighed herskede blandt borgerne, og hver mand skammede sig over at stemme offentligt for et uretfærdigt forslag eller en uværdig kandidat; men da folket blev fordærvet, og stemmer blev købt, var det passende, at afstemningen skulle være hemmelig, så købere kunne tøjles af mistillid, og slyngler gives midler til ikke at være forrædere.

danishChanges.before: Det degenererer til tyranni, når det tilrøver sig den udøvende magt, som det burde indskrænke sig til at tøjle, og når det forsøger at se bort fra lovene, som det burde indskrænke sig til at beskytte. Eforernes umådelige magt, der var ufarlig, så længe Sparta bevarede sin moral, fremskyndede fordærvet, da fordærvet først var sat ind. Blodet af Agis, slagtet af disse tyranner, blev hævnet af hans efterfølger; eforernes forbrydelse og straf fremskyndede begge republikkens ødelæggelse, og efter Kleomenes ophørte Sparta med at have nogen betydning. Roma gik til grunde på samme måde: den overdrevne magt hos tribunerne, som de gradvis havde tilrøvet sig, tjente til sidst — ved hjælp af love lavet for at sikre frihed — som beskyttelse for de kejsere, der ødelagde den. Hvad angår De Tis Råd i Venedig, er det en bloddomstol, en genstand for rædsel for både patriciere og folk; langt fra at give lovene ophøjet beskyttelse gør det intet — nu hvor lovene er nedværdiget — andet end at slå i mørke slag, som ingen vover at lægge mærke til.
danishChanges.after: Det degenererer til tyranni, når det tilrøver sig den udøvende magt, som det burde indskrænke sig til at tøjle, og når det forsøger at se bort fra lovene, som det burde indskrænke sig til at beskytte. Eforernes umådelige magt, der var ufarlig, så længe Sparta bevarede sin moral, fremskyndede fordærvet, da fordærvet først var sat ind. Blodet af Agis, slagtet af disse tyranner, blev hævnet af hans efterfølger; eforernes forbrydelse og straf fremskyndede begge republikkens ødelæggelse, og efter Kleomenes ophørte Sparta med at have nogen betydning. Rom gik til grunde på samme måde: den overdrevne magt hos tribunerne, som de gradvis havde tilrøvet sig, tjente til sidst — ved hjælp af love lavet for at sikre frihed — som beskyttelse for de kejsere, der ødelagde den. Hvad angår De Tis Råd i Venedig, er det en bloddomstol, en genstand for rædsel for både patriciere og folk; langt fra at give lovene ophøjet beskyttelse gør det intet — nu hvor lovene er nedværdiget — andet end at rette slag i mørket, som ingen vover at lægge mærke til.
reasons: Standard Danish place name
French fidelity, idiomatic modern Danish, complete notes

Disse intervaller, der ikke bør være lange nok til at give misbrug tid til at slå rod, kan fastsættes ved lov på en måde, der tillader, at de let kan forkortes ved behov ved hjælp af ekstraordinære kommissioner.

danishChanges.before: Hvis en forøgelse af regeringens aktivitet er et tilstrækkeligt lægemiddel, koncentreres magten i hænderne på en eller to af dens medlemmer. Hvis faren på den anden side er sådan, at lovenes apparat selv er en hindring for deres egen bevarelse, er metoden at udnævne en øverste hersker, der skal lukke munden på alle lovene og suspendere, et øjeblik, den suveræne myndighed. danishChanges.before: I stedet nøjedes senatet med at betro hele sin magt til konsulerne, så Cicero for at handle effektivt på et hovedpunkt blev tvunget til at overskride sine beføjelser; og selv om hans adfærd i de første glædestransporter blev billiget, blev han med rette senere kaldt til regnskab for blodet af borgere udgydt i strid med lovene. danishChanges.before: Det er nyttesløst at skelne en nations moral fra genstandene for dens agtelse; begge afhænger af samme princip og er nødvendigvis uadskillelige. Der findes ikke noget folk på jorden, hvis valg af fornøjelser ikke afgøres af mening snarere end af natur. Sæt mænds meninger ret, og deres moral vil rense sig selv. Mænd elsker altid det, der er godt, eller det, de finder godt; det er i bedømmelsen af, hvad der er godt, at de tager fejl. Det er altså denne dømmekraft, der må reguleres. Brugen af sekundanter i dueller, der var blevet drevet til vilde yderligheder i Frankrigs kongerige, blev gjort til at med disse blotte ord i et kongeligt edikt: »Hvad angår dem, der er kujoner nok til at tilkalde sekundanter.« Denne dom, der foregreb offentlighedens, fastlagde den pludselig. Men da edikter fra samme kilde forsøgte at erklære duellering selv som en handling af fejhed — sådan som den virkelig er — så tog offentligheden, eftersom den almindelige mening ikke betragtede den som sådan, ingen notits af en afgørelse på et punkt, hvorpå dens sind allerede var gjort op.

Politisk krig var også teologisk krig; gudernes provinser var, så at sige, fastsat af nationernes grænser. Det ene folks gud havde ingen rettigheder over et andet. Hedningernes guder var ikke nidkære guder; de delte verdens imperium imellem sig: selv Moses og hebræerne gav sig undertiden til denne opfattelse ved at tale om Israels Gud. De betragtede ganske vist kanaanæernes guder som magtesløse, et fordømt folk dømt til ødelæggelse, hvis plads de skulle tage; men husk, hvordan de talte om opdelingerne af nabofolk, de havde forbud mod at angribe! »Er besiddelsen af, hvad der tilhører din gud Kemosj, ikke retmæssigt din?« sagde Jefta til ammonitterne. »Vi har samme adkomst til de jorder, vor sejrende Gud har gjort til sine egne.«[1] Her er der, tror jeg, en anerkendelse af, at Kemosjs rettigheder og Israels Guds rettigheder er af samme natur.

danishChanges.before: Hver religion, der altså udelukkende var knyttet til lovene i den stat, der foreskrev den, var der ingen måde at omvende et folk på, undtagen ved at gøre det til slave, og der kunne ikke være andre missionærer end erobrere. Da forpligtelsen til at ændre kult var den lov, hvorunder den besejrede bøjede sig, måtte sejren komme, før en sådan ændring kunne foreslås. Langt fra at mænd kæmpede for guderne, kæmpede guderne, som hos Homer, for mænd; hver side bad sin gud om sejr og betalte ham med nye altre. Inden de tog en by, indkaldte romerne dens guder til at forlade den; og når de lod tarentinerne beholde deres krænkede guder, betragtede de disse guder som underkastet deres egne og forpligtede til at vise dem hyldest. De lod de besejrede beholde deres guder, som de lod dem beholde deres love. En krans til Capitols Jupiter var ofte den eneste tribut, de pålagde.

danishChanges.before: Det var under disse omstændigheder, at Jesus kom for at oprette et åndeligt rige på jorden, der ved at adskille det teologiske fra det politiske system gjorde, at staten ikke længere var én, og frembragte de indre opdelinger, der aldrig er ophørt med at plage kristne folk. Da den nye idé om et rige af den anden verden aldrig kunne være faldet hedninger ind, så de altid på de kristne som virkelige oprørere, der, mens de foregav at underkaste sig, kun ventede på en chance for at gøre sig uafhængige og deres herrer og ved kløgt at tilrane sig den myndighed, de under deres svaghed lod, som om de respekterede. danishChanges.before: Adskillige folk har dog, selv i Europa og dets nabolag, ønsket uden held at bevare eller genoprette det gamle system; men kristendommens ånd har sejret overalt. Den hellige kult er altid forblevet eller atter blevet uafhængig af suverænen, og der har ikke været noget nødvendigt bånd mellem den og statens krop. Muhammed havde meget sunde synspunkter og bandt sit politiske system godt sammen; og så længe hans regerings form fortsatte under de kalifer, der efterfulgte ham, var den regering ganske rigtigt én og i den udstrækning god. Men araberne, der var blevet velstående, lærde, civiliserede, slappe og fejge, blev erobret af barbarer: opdelingen mellem de to magter begyndte igen; og selv om den er mindre åbenlys blandt muhammedanerne end blandt de kristne, eksisterer den ikke desto mindre, særligt i Alis sekt, og der findes stater, såsom Persien, hvor den uafladeligt mærkes.

danishChanges.before: Jeg tror, at hvis studiet af historien blev udviklet fra dette synspunkt, ville det være let at gendrive de modsatte meninger fra Bayle og Warburton, hvoraf den ene fastholder, at religion ikke kan være til nogen nytte for den politiske krop, mens den anden tværtimod fastholder, at kristendommen er dens stærkeste støtte. Vi kunne vise den første, at ingen stat nogensinde er blevet grundlagt uden et religiøst grundlag, og den anden, at kristendommens lov i bund og grund gør mere skade ved at svække end gavn ved at styrke statens forfatning. For at gøre mig forståelig behøver jeg blot at gøre de alt for vage idéer om religion, der angår dette emne, lidt mere præcise.

danishChanges.before: Religionen, betragtet i forhold til samfundet — der enten er almen eller særlig — kan også deles i to slags: menneskets religion og borgerens. Den første, der hverken har templer eller altre eller riter, og som er begrænset til den rent indre kult af den øverste Gud og moralens evige forpligtelser, er Evangeliets religion ren og enkel, den sande teisme — hvad der kan kaldes naturlig guddommelig ret eller lov. Den anden, kodificeret i et enkelt land, giver det dets guder, dets egne værneherrer; den har sine dogmer, sine riter og sin ydre kult foreskrevet ved lov; uden for den enkelte nation, der følger den, er hele verden i dens øjne vantro, fremmed og barbarisk; menneskets pligter og rettigheder strækker sig for den kun så langt som dens egne altre. Af denne slags var alle de tidlige folks religioner, som vi kan definere som borgerlig eller positiv guddommelig ret eller lov.

Den er igen dårlig, når den bliver tyrannisk og udelukkende og gør et folk blodtørstigt og intolerant, så det ånder ild og slagtning og betragter drabet på enhver, der ikke tror på dets guder, som en hellig handling. danishChanges.before: Vi får at vide, at et folk af sande kristne ville danne det mest fuldkomne samfund, der kan tænkes. Jeg ser i denne antagelse kun én stor vanskelighed: et samfund af sande kristne ville ikke være et samfund af mænd.

danishChanges.before: For at staten skal være fredfyldt, og harmoni opretholdes, måtte alle borgerne uden undtagelse være gode kristne; hvis der ved uheld var en enkelt egennyttig eller hykler — en Catilina eller en Cromwell, for eksempel — ville han bestemt få overtaget over sine fromme landsmænd. Kristen kærlighed tillader ikke let en mand at tænke ondt om sine næster. Så snart han ved et eller andet trick har opdaget kunsten at narre dem og få fat i en del af den offentlige myndighed, har man en mand etableret i værdighed; det er Guds vilje, at han respekteres. Meget snart har man en magt; det er Guds vilje, at den adlydes: og hvis magten misbruges af den, der udøver den, er det den svøbe, hvormed Gud straffer sine børn. Det vigtige er at komme i himlen, og resignation er blot endnu et middel til at gøre det.

danishChanges.before: Hvis krig bryder ud med en anden stat, marcherer borgerne villigt ud i kamp; ikke en eneste af dem tænker på at flygte; de gør deres pligt, men de har ingen lidenskab for sejren; de ved bedre, hvordan de skal dø, end hvordan de skal sejre. Hvad betyder det, om de vinder eller taber? Ved Forsynet ikke bedre end de, hvad der er passende for dem? englishChanges.after:
_Author’s prefatory notice_

This short treatise is an extract from a larger work, begun some time ago without measuring my abilities and long since abandoned. Of the various pieces that could be taken from what was completed, this is the most substantial and seemed to me the least unworthy of being offered to the public. The rest no longer exists.

_Book I_

I want to ask whether, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule of administration — taking men as they are and laws as they might be. In this inquiry I will always try to unite what right sanctions with what is prescribed by interest, so that justice and utility are never divided.
reasons: Restore complete French Avertissement in first slot, explicitly labeled; preserve exact chapter/paragraph slots

englishChanges.before: If I considered only force and the effects derived from it, I would say: “As long as a people is compelled to obey, and obeys, it does well; as soon as it can shake off the yoke and does so, it does still better — for in regaining its liberty by the same right that took it away, either the people is justified in taking it back, or there was no justification for those who took it in the first place.” But the social order is a sacred right that serves as the basis of every other right. This right, however, does not come from nature: it must therefore be founded on conventions. Before coming to that, I have to prove what I have just asserted.

This right, however, does not come from nature: it must therefore be founded on conventions. The question is what these conventions are. Before coming to that, I have to prove what I have just asserted.

englishChanges.before: modern times: most people mistake a town for a city and a townsman for a citizen. They do not realize that houses make a town, but citizens a city. The Carthaginians long ago paid dearly for this same mistake. I have never read of the title of citizen being given to the subjects of any prince — not even the ancient Macedonians, nor the English of today, though they are nearer to liberty than anyone else. The French alone everywhere casually adopt the name of citizens, because, as their dictionaries show, they have no idea what it means; otherwise they would, in usurping it, be guilty of the crime of _lèse-majesté_. Among them, the name expresses a virtue, not a right. When Bodin spoke of our citizens and townsmen, he made a serious blunder by mistaking the one for the other. M. d’Alembert avoided the error: in his article on Geneva, he clearly distinguished the four orders of men (or even five, counting mere foreigners) who live in our town, of which only two compose the Republic. No other French writer, to my knowledge, has grasped the real meaning of the word citizen.
englishChanges.after: [1] The real meaning of this word has been almost wholly lost in modern times; most people mistake a town for a city, and a townsman for a citizen. They do not know that houses make a town, but citizens a city. The same mistake long ago cost the Carthaginians dear. I have never read of the title of citizens being given to the subjects of any prince, not even the ancient Macedonians or the English of today, though they are nearer liberty than anyone else. The French alone everywhere familiarly adopt the name of citizens, because, as can be seen from their dictionaries, they have no idea of its meaning; otherwise they would be guilty in usurping it, of the crime of _lèse-majesté_: among them, the name expresses a virtue, and not a right. When Bodin spoke of our citizens and townsmen, he fell into a bad blunder in taking the one class for the other. M. d'Alembert has avoided the error, and, in his article on Geneva, has clearly distinguished the four orders of men (or even five, counting mere foreigners) who dwell in our town, of which two only compose the Republic. No other French writer, to my knowledge, has understood the real meaning of the word citizen.

englishChanges.before: In granting the right of first occupancy to necessity and labor, are we not really stretching it as far as it can go? Can such a right be left unlimited? Is it enough to set foot on a plot of common ground to claim instantly to be its master? Is it enough that a man has the strength to drive others off for a moment to establish his right to keep them away forever? How can a man or a people seize an immense territory and shut it off from the rest of the world, except by a punishable usurpation, since by such an act all others are robbed of the dwelling place and the means of subsistence that nature gave them in common? When Nuñez Balbao, standing on the seashore, took possession of the South Seas and the whole of South America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess all their actual inhabitants and shut them out from every prince of the world? On that reasoning, these ceremonies are pointlessly multiplied, and the Catholic King need only take possession all at once, from his apartment, of the whole universe — making a subsequent reservation only for whatever was already in the possession of other princes.

When Nuñez Balboa, standing on the seashore, took possession of the South Seas and the whole of South America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess all their actual inhabitants and exclude every prince in the world from those territories? On that reasoning, these ceremonies are pointlessly multiplied, and the Catholic King need only take possession all at once, from his apartment, of the whole universe — making a subsequent reservation only for whatever was already in the possession of other princes.
reasons: French primary spelling.
French en exclure tous les princes: exclude princes, not inhabitants from princes.

englishChanges.before: I shall end this chapter and this book by remarking on a fact on which the whole social system should rest: namely, that, far from destroying natural inequality, the fundamental compact substitutes a moral and legitimate equality for whatever physical inequality nature may have set up among men, and that men, who may be unequal in strength or intelligence, all become equal by convention and by legal right.[1]

englishChanges.before: In reality, while it is not impossible for a particular will to coincide with the general will on some point, it is at least impossible for the agreement to be lasting and constant; for the particular will tends, by its very nature, toward partiality, while the general will tends toward equality. It is even more impossible to have any guarantee of this agreement; for even if it always existed, it would be the effect not of art but of chance. The Sovereign may indeed say: “I now actually will what this man wills, or at least what he says he wills”; but it cannot say: “What he wills tomorrow, I shall also will” — for it is absurd for the will to bind itself for the future, and no will is required to consent to anything that is not for the good of the being who wills. So if the people simply promises to obey, by that very act it dissolves itself and loses what makes it a people; the moment a master exists, there is no longer a Sovereign, and from that moment the body politic has ceased to exist.

englishChanges.before: The right of pardoning, or exempting the guilty from a penalty imposed by the law and pronounced by the judge, belongs only to the authority that is superior to both judge and law — namely, the Sovereign. Even the Sovereign’s right in this matter is far from clear, and the cases for exercising it are extremely rare. In a well-governed State there are few punishments, not because there are many pardons, but because criminals are rare; it is when a State is in decay that the multitude of crimes guarantees impunity. Under the Roman Republic, neither the Senate nor the Consuls ever attempted to pardon; even the people never did, though it sometimes revoked its own decision. Frequent pardons mean that crime will soon no longer need them, and anyone can see where that leads. But I feel my heart protesting and holding back my pen; let us leave such questions to the just man who has never offended, and who would himself stand in no need of pardon.

englishChanges.before: I have already said that there can be no general will directed at a particular object. Such an object must be either inside or outside the State. If outside, then a will alien to the State cannot be general in relation to it; if inside, it is part of the State, and a relation then arises between whole and part that makes them two separate beings — the part being one, and the whole minus the part being the other. But the whole minus a part is not the whole; and as long as this relation persists, there is no whole, only two unequal parts; from which it follows that the will of the one is no longer in any respect general in relation to the other.

englishChanges.before: This sublime reason, far above the reach of the common crowd, is what the legislator puts in the mouth of the immortals, in order to constrain by divine authority those whom human prudence could not move.[4] But not just anyone can make the gods speak, or get himself believed when he proclaims himself their interpreter. The great soul of the legislator is the only miracle that can prove his mission. Any man can engrave tablets of stone, or buy an oracle, or pretend to secret communion with some divinity, or train a bird to whisper in his ear, or find other vulgar tricks to impose on the people. The man whose knowledge goes no further may indeed gather a band of fools around him, but he will never found an empire, and his extravagances will quickly perish with him. Empty tricks form a passing tie; only wisdom can make it lasting. The Judaic law, which still endures, and the law of the child of Ishmael, which has ruled half the world for ten centuries, still proclaim the great men who laid them down; and while the pride of philosophy or the blind spirit of faction sees in them nothing but lucky impostures, the true political theorist admires, in the institutions they set up, the great and powerful genius that presides over things made to endure.

englishChanges.before: A thousand arguments could be given for this principle. First, long distances make administration more difficult, just as a weight grows heavier at the end of a longer lever. Administration becomes more and more burdensome as distance increases; for, in the first place, each city has its own administration, paid for by the people; each district has its own, still paid for by the people; then comes each province, and then the great governments, satrapies, and viceroyalties, costing more the higher you go, and always at the expense of the unfortunate people. Last comes the supreme administration, which eclipses all the rest. All these added burdens are a continual drain on the subjects; far from being better governed by all these layers of authority, they are worse governed than they would be under a single one. Meanwhile, scarcely enough resources remain to meet emergencies; and when those have to be drawn on, the State is always on the brink of destruction.
englishChanges.after: A thousand arguments could be given for this principle. First, long distances make administration more difficult, just as a weight grows heavier at the end of a longer lever. Administration becomes more and more burdensome as administrative levels multiply; for, in the first place, each city has its own administration, paid for by the people; each district has its own, still paid for by the people; then comes each province, and then the great governments, satrapies, and viceroyalties, costing more the higher you go, and always at the expense of the unfortunate people. Last comes the supreme administration, which crushes everything beneath it. All these added burdens are a continual drain on the subjects; far from being better governed by all these layers of authority, they are worse governed than they would be under a single one. Meanwhile, scarcely enough resources remain to meet emergencies; and when those have to be drawn on, the State is always on the brink of destruction.
reasons: French à mesure que les degrés se multiplient; distance was preceding distinct reason.
French qui écrase tout: crushing financial burden, not merely eclipsing.

englishChanges.before: But these general aims of every good legislative system need to be modified in each country according to the local situation and the temperament of the inhabitants; and these circumstances should determine, in each case, the particular system of institutions that is best — not perhaps in itself, but for the State for which it is intended. If, for instance, the soil is barren and unproductive, or the land too crowded for its inhabitants, the people should turn to industry and the crafts, and exchange what they produce for the goods they lack. If, on the other hand, a people lives on rich plains and fertile slopes, or, in a good land, lacks inhabitants, it should give all its attention to agriculture, which causes men to multiply, and should drive out the crafts, which would only result in depopulation by clustering the few inhabitants there are in a few localities.[2] If a nation lives on an extensive and convenient coastline, let it cover the sea with ships and foster commerce and navigation. It will have a life that is short and glorious. If, on its coasts, the sea washes nothing but nearly inaccessible rocks, let it remain barbarous and ichthyophagous: it will have a quieter, perhaps a better, and certainly a happier life. In a word, beyond the principles common to all, every nation has within itself something that gives those principles a particular application, and makes its legislation peculiarly its own. So among the Jews long ago, and more recently among the Arabs, the chief object was religion; among the Athenians, letters; at Carthage and Tyre, commerce; at Rhodes, shipping; at Sparta, war; at Rome, virtue. The author of _The Spirit of the Laws_ has shown with many examples by what art the legislator directs the constitution toward each of these objects.

englishChanges.before: The laws regulating this relation bear the name of political laws, and are also called fundamental laws — not without reason, if they are wise. For if there is in each State only one good system, the people that has it should hold fast to it; but if the established order is bad, why should laws that prevent men from being good be regarded as fundamental? englishChanges.before: Along with these three kinds of law goes a fourth, the most important of all, which is engraved not on tablets of marble or brass but on the hearts of the citizens. This forms the real constitution of the State; takes on new powers each day; restores the others or takes their place when they decay or die out; keeps a people on the path it was meant to follow; and silently replaces authority with the force of habit. I am speaking of morality, of custom, above all of public opinion — a power unknown to political thinkers, on which nevertheless the success of everything else depends. With this the great legislator concerns himself in secret, even while he seems to confine himself to particular regulations; for these are only the arc of the arch, while manners and morals, slower to take shape, in the end form its immovable keystone.

englishChanges.before: The members of this body are called magistrates or _kings_ — that is, _governors_ — and the body as a whole bears the name _prince_.[1] Those who hold that the act by which a people places itself under a prince is not a contract are therefore right. It is simply and solely a commission, an employment, in which the rulers, as mere officials of the Sovereign, exercise in their own name the power of which it makes them trustees. This power can be limited, modified, or revoked at the Sovereign’s pleasure; for the alienation of such a right is incompatible with the nature of the social body, and contrary to the end of association.

englishChanges.before: It follows from this double relation that the continuous proportion between Sovereign, prince, and people is by no means an arbitrary idea, but a necessary consequence of the nature of the body politic. It also follows that, since one of the extreme terms — the people, as subject — is fixed and represented by unity, whenever the duplicate ratio rises or falls, the simple ratio does the same and is changed accordingly. From this we see that there is no single absolute form of government, but as many governments differing in nature as there are States differing in size.

This gives rise to a new proportion, within which is yet another, depending on the arrangement of the magistracies, until an indivisible middle term is reached: a single ruler or supreme magistrate, who can be represented, in the middle of this progression, as the unit between the fractional and the ordinal series.

englishChanges.before: We found, on general grounds, that monarchy is suitable only for great States, and this is confirmed when we examine it on its own. The more numerous the public administration, the smaller the relation between the prince and his subjects, and the closer it comes to equality, so that in democracy the ratio is unity, or absolute equality. As the government is restricted in number, the ratio increases and reaches its _maximum_ when the government is in the hands of a single person. There is then too great a distance between prince and people, and the State lacks a bond of union. To form such a bond, there must be intermediate orders, with princes, dignitaries, and nobility to make them up. But none of this suits a small State, where all class differences mean ruin.
englishChanges.after: We found, on general grounds, that monarchy is suitable only for great States, and this is confirmed when we examine it on its own. englishChanges.before: For a monarchical State to have any chance of being well governed, its population and extent must be proportionate to the abilities of its governor. It is easier to conquer than to rule. With a long enough lever, the world could be moved by a single finger; but to hold it up requires the shoulders of Hercules. However small a State may be, the prince is hardly ever big enough for it. When, on the other hand, the State is too small for its ruler, in those rare cases too it is badly governed, because the ruler, constantly pursuing his great designs, forgets the interests of the people, and makes them no less wretched by misusing the talents he has than a less able ruler would by lacking them. A kingdom should, so to speak, expand or contract with each reign, depending on the prince’s capabilities; but since the abilities of a senate are more constant in quantity, the State can have permanent borders without the administration suffering.
englishChanges.after: For a monarchical State to have any chance of being well governed, its size or extent must be proportionate to the abilities of its governor. It is easier to conquer than to rule. With a long enough lever, the world could be moved by a single finger; but to hold it up requires the shoulders of Hercules. As soon as a State is at all large, the prince is hardly ever big enough for it. When, on the other hand, the State is too small for its ruler, in those rare cases too it is badly governed, because the ruler, constantly pursuing his great designs, forgets the interests of the people, and makes them no less wretched by misusing the talents he has than a less able ruler would by lacking them. A kingdom should, so to speak, expand or contract with each reign, depending on the prince’s capabilities; but since the abilities of a senate are more constant in quantity, the State can have permanent borders without the administration suffering.

englishChanges.before: the preference for human prosperity. Those countries in which letters and arts have flourished have been too much admired, because the hidden object of their cultivation has not been understood, and their fatal effects not taken into account. “Idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset.” [“Fools called ‘humanity’ what was a part of slavery,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Shall we never see, in the maxims books lay down, the vulgar interest that prompts their writers? No: whatever they say, when, despite its renown, a country is depopulated, it is not true that all is well, and it is not enough that a poet should have an income of 100,000 francs to make his age the best of all. Less attention should be paid to the apparent repose and tranquility of the rulers than to the well-being of their nations as wholes, and above all of the most populous States. A hailstorm lays waste several cantons, but rarely brings on a famine. Outbreaks and civil wars give rulers rude shocks, but they are not the real ills of peoples, who may even get a respite while there is a dispute over who shall tyrannize them. Their true prosperity and calamities come from their permanent condition: it is when the whole remains crushed beneath the yoke that decay sets in, and the rulers destroy the people at will, and “ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant” [“Where they create a desert, they call it peace,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] When the squabbles of the great disturbed the kingdom of France, and the Coadjutor of Paris carried a dagger in his pocket to the Parliament, these things did not prevent the people of France from prospering and multiplying in dignity, ease, and freedom. Long ago Greece flourished in the midst of the most savage wars; blood ran in torrents, and yet the whole country was full of inhabitants. It seemed, says Machiavelli, that in the midst of murder, proscription, and civil war, our republic only thrived: the virtue, morality, and independence of the citizens did more to strengthen it than all their dissensions did to weaken it. A little disturbance gives the soul elasticity; what makes the race truly prosperous is not so much peace as liberty.

englishChanges.before: It is also true that, in such cases, one cannot be too careful to observe all the formalities required to distinguish a regular and legitimate act from a seditious tumult, and the will of a whole people from the clamor of a faction. Here above all, no further concession should be made to the awkward possibility than cannot, in the strictest logic, be refused. From this obligation the prince derives a great advantage in keeping his power against the people, without anyone being able to say he has usurped it. Seeming to avail himself only of his rights, he finds it very easy to extend them, and to prevent — under the pretext of keeping the peace — assemblies whose purpose is to re-establish order. Thus he takes advantage of a silence he does not allow to be broken, or of irregularities he himself causes, to assume that he has the support of those whom fear keeps from speaking, and to punish those who dare to speak. So it was that the decemvirs, first elected for one year and then kept on for a second, tried to perpetuate their power by forbidding the comitia to assemble. By this easy method, every government in the world, once clothed in public power, sooner or later usurps the sovereign authority.

[1] I say “in the Campus Martius” because that was where the comitia assembled by centuries; in its two other forms, the people assembled in the _forum_ or elsewhere; and then the _capite censi_ had as much influence and authority as the foremost citizens.

[2] _Custodes, diribitores, rogatores suffragiorum_.

englishChanges.before: If increasing the activity of the government is a sufficient remedy, power is concentrated in the hands of one or two of its members. In this case the change is not in the authority of the laws, but only in the form of administering them. If, on the other hand, the danger is such that the apparatus of the laws is itself an obstacle to their own preservation, the method is to nominate a supreme ruler who shall silence all the laws and suspend, for a moment, the sovereign authority. In such a case, there is no doubt about the general will, and it is clear that the people’s first intention is that the State should not perish. So suspending the legislative authority is in no way abolishing it; the magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak; he dominates it, but cannot represent it. He can do anything, except make laws.
englishChanges.after: If increasing the activity of the government is a sufficient remedy, power is concentrated in the hands of one or two of its members. In this case the change is not in the authority of the laws, but only in the form of administering them. If, on the other hand, the danger is such that the apparatus of the laws is itself an obstacle to protection against the danger, the method is to nominate a supreme ruler who shall silence all the laws and suspend, for a moment, the sovereign authority. In such a case, there is no doubt about the general will, and it is clear that the people’s first intention is that the State should not perish. So suspending the legislative authority is in no way abolishing it; the magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak; he dominates it, but cannot represent it. He can do anything, except make laws.
reasons: French s’en garantir refers to danger, not preserving laws

englishChanges.before: It is useless to distinguish a nation’s morality from the objects of its esteem; both depend on the same principle and are necessarily inseparable. There is no people on earth whose choice of pleasures is not decided by opinion rather than by nature. Set right men’s opinions, and their morality will purge itself. Men always love what is good, or what they find good; it is in judging what is good that they go wrong. This judgment, then, is what must be regulated. Whoever judges of morality judges of honor; and whoever judges of honor finds his law in opinion.

englishChanges.before: If asked how, in pagan times, when each State had its own cult and its own gods, there were no wars of religion, I answer that it was precisely because each State, having its own cult as well as its own government, made no distinction between its gods and its laws. Political war was also theological war; the provinces of the gods were, so to speak, fixed by the borders of nations. The god of one people had no rights over another. The gods of the pagans were not jealous gods; they shared the empire of the world among themselves: even Moses and the Hebrews sometimes lent themselves to this view by speaking of the God of Israel. They regarded as powerless, it is true, the gods of the Canaanites, a proscribed people condemned to destruction, whose place they were to take; but remember how they spoke of the divisions of neighboring peoples they were forbidden to attack! “Is not the possession of what belongs to your god Chamos lawfully your due?” said Jephthah to the Ammonites. “We have the same title to the lands our conquering God has made his own.”[1] Here, I think, there is a recognition that the rights of Chamos and those of the God of Israel are of the same nature.
englishChanges.after: If asked how, in pagan times, when each State had its own cult and its own gods, there were no wars of religion, I answer that it was precisely because each State, having its own cult as well as its own government, made no distinction between its gods and its laws. The gods of the pagans were not jealous gods; they shared the empire of the world among themselves: even Moses and the Hebrews sometimes lent themselves to this view by speaking of the God of Israel. They regarded as powerless, it is true, the gods of the Canaanites, a proscribed people condemned to destruction, whose place they were to take; but remember how they spoke of the divinities of neighboring peoples they were forbidden to attack! “Is not the possession of what belongs to your god Chamos lawfully your due?” said Jephthah to the Ammonites. “We have the same title to the lands our conquering God has made his own.”[1] Here, I think, there is a recognition that the rights of Chamos and those of the God of Israel are of the same nature.

englishChanges.before: Among us, the Kings of England have made themselves heads of the Church, and the Czars have done the same; but this title has made them less its masters than its ministers; they have gained not so much the right to change it as the power to maintain it: they are not its legislators, but only its princes. Wherever the clergy is a corporate body,[3] it is master and legislator in its own country. There are thus two powers, two Sovereigns, in England and in Russia, as well as elsewhere.

englishChanges.before: But, setting aside political considerations, let us come back to what is right, and settle our principles on this important point. The right that the social compact gives the Sovereign over the subjects does not, as we have seen, exceed the limits of public expediency.[5] The subjects, then, owe the Sovereign an account of their opinions only insofar as they matter to the community. Now, it matters very much to the community that each citizen should have a religion. That will make him love his duty; but the dogmas of that religion concern the State and its members only insofar as they bear on morality and on the duties he who professes them is bound to perform toward others. Each man may have, beyond that, whatever opinions he pleases, without it being the Sovereign’s business to take notice; for since the Sovereign has no authority in the other world, whatever the lot of its subjects may be in the life to come, that is not its business, provided they are good citizens in this life.
englishChanges.after: But, setting aside political considerations, let us come back to what is right, and settle our principles on this important point. Now, it matters very much to the community that each citizen should have a religion that makes him love his duties; but the dogmas of that religion concern the State and its members only insofar as they bear on morality and on the duties he who professes them is bound to perform toward others. englishChanges.before: without which society cannot even subsist. Suppose a body of clergy were to claim the sole right of permitting this act — a right every intolerant religion must necessarily claim — is it not clear that, in establishing the authority of the Church in this respect, it will be destroying that of the prince, who will from then on have only as many subjects as the clergy choose to allow him? Being in a position to marry or not to marry people according to their acceptance of such-and-such a doctrine, their admission or rejection of such-and-such a formula, their greater or lesser piety, the Church alone, by the exercise of prudence and firmness, will dispose of all inheritances, offices, and citizens, and even of the State itself, which could not subsist if it were composed entirely of bastards. But, I shall be told, there will be appeals on the ground of abuse, summonses, and decrees; the temporalities will be seized. How sad! The clergy, however little — I will not say courage, but sense — it has, will take no notice and go its way: it will quietly allow appeals, summonses, decrees, and seizures, and in the end will remain the master. It is not, I think, a great sacrifice to give up a part when one is sure of securing the whole.
